Title: Email not working after a DNS change? Here's how to fix it fast
Sales pitch: When email stops working after a DNS change, it's usually due to missing MX and related records, not lost data. Recreate these essential records at your new DNS host to restore mail flow.
Main Pain Point: Email services failing after a domain's DNS or nameserver settings have been changed.
Solution: Identify missing DNS records (especially MX, SPF, DKIM) after a nameserver change and restore them at the new DNS host to re-establish proper mail routing and sending.
Summary: This article addresses the common issue of email services becoming unavailable after a domain's DNS or nameserver settings are changed. The primary takeaway is that such disruptions are almost always caused by missing or incorrectly configured DNS records, particularly MX (Mail Exchanger) and supporting records like SPF, DKIM, and A records, rather than lost email data. When nameservers are updated, DNS control transfers to a new provider, and these crucial records do not migrate automatically, leaving incoming mail with nowhere to be routed. The article guides readers through a systematic troubleshooting process: first, confirming that the issue is indeed DNS-related by checking timing, attempting webmail logins, and testing both sending and receiving. It then explains how to identify which specific records are missing or incorrect by comparing the current DNS zone with the email provider's requirements, using tools like MxToolbox. The solution involves recreating the necessary MX, SPF, DKIM, and other relevant records at the new DNS host. It clarifies that mailboxes and existing messages reside on the mail server, unaffected by DNS changes, and that propagation can take up to 48 hours. By accurately restoring these records, users can effectively resolve email delivery and sending problems post-DNS migration, ensuring business continuity.

Title: Email CTR vs CTOR: Yes, they're different
Sales pitch: Understand the crucial difference between Email CTR and CTOR to accurately measure campaign success. Stop misinterpreting metrics and gain actionable insights for better email marketing performance.
Features Mentioned: Website Builders & Design; AI & Automation; Email & Marketing Automation
Main Pain Point: Confusion and misinterpretation of email marketing metrics, specifically CTR vs. CTOR, leading to inaccurate assessments of campaign effectiveness.
Solution: Clearly differentiate between CTR (clicks divided by delivered emails) and CTOR (clicks divided by opened emails), understand what each metric signifies, and track trends within the context of one's own business and list size rather than relying solely on broad industry averages.
Target audience: Marketers & Content Teams; Site Owners & Non-Technical Users
Summary: This article clarifies the distinction between Email Click-Through Rate (CTR) and Click-to-Open Rate (CTOR), two critical but often confused email marketing metrics. The main takeaway is that these metrics measure different aspects of campaign performance and are not interchangeable. CTR, calculated by dividing total clicks by the number of emails delivered, indicates the overall effectiveness of an email in driving action from the entire recipient list, including subject line, preview text, and content. CTOR, calculated by dividing clicks by the number of emails opened, measures how engaging the content is once the email has been opened. The article explains that benchmarks vary significantly based on list size, industry, and business stage, advising readers to focus on their own performance trends rather than external averages. It highlights that CTR is useful for diagnosing deliverability issues, while CTOR is better for evaluating content effectiveness. By understanding and correctly applying these metrics, marketers can gain more accurate insights into their campaigns, enabling them to make informed decisions to improve engagement and drive better results.
